title: Androcles and the Lion

setting.period: The Roman Empire, about 2,000 years ago

provenance.tradition: Roman tale, first written down by Aulus Gellius
provenance.rights: The text is our own retelling of a traditional Roman tale, written for Omramo; it does not use the wording of the cited edition. The cited edition is in the US public domain (published before 1931); other territories not verified. Legal review pending (PRD Q23).

geography.lesson: The Roman Empire lay all round the Mediterranean Sea. The story travels from the dry hills of Roman North Africa, across the sea by grain ship, to the city of Rome.

culture.lesson: Rome gathered in huge arenas to watch shows, and some people in the Roman world were owned as slaves; both are said plainly and briefly. The tale itself comes from a Roman writer, Aulus Gellius, and nobody can check it now.

moral.lesson: A kindness done when you are afraid, with nobody watching, can come back years later. The lion remembers, and so in the end do the people of Rome.
moral.reflectionQuestion: Androcles was frightened of the lion and helped him anyway. What made him do it, do you think?

moral: A kindness is never forgotten, by people or by animals.

cover.alt: A man in a rough tunic kneels and holds the big paw of a dark-maned lion in his lap, at the mouth of a cave in warm ochre rock.

card.label: Character · a runaway baker
card.title: Androcles
card.body: He runs from a hard master with nothing but an empty water skin. When a hurt lion holds out its paw, he is frightened, and he helps all the same.
card.portraitAlt: Androcles, a wiry man with dark curly hair and a short beard, in a rough pale tunic, holding a long thorn between finger and thumb.

card.label: Character · a lion of the hills
card.title: The Lion
card.body: He is a Barbary lion, the big dark-maned kind that once lived wild in North Africa. His roar shakes dust from a roof, and he remembers a friend for years.
card.portraitAlt: The Lion sitting up with his dark mane round his face, holding out one big front paw wrapped in a strip of pale cloth.

tapTargets.title: Slavery
tapTargets.line: A slave was a person owned by someone else and made to work without pay.

cultureNote.label: From ancient Rome
cultureNote.text: In the Roman world many people were owned by others and could not choose their work or leave. It was wrong then, and today it is against the law in every country.

tapTargets.pictureAlt: A plain iron bar lying beside a heavy wooden gate that stands a little open, with morning light coming through the gap.

framingDevice.label: FIND IT ON THE MAP
framingDevice.line: Rome’s empire reached all the way round the sea. In another of its cities, Ephesus, stood a temple so grand that people called it a Wonder of the World.

tapTargets.title: North Africa
tapTargets.line: The lands along the south shore of the Mediterranean Sea, across the water from Italy.

cultureNote.label: From North Africa
cultureNote.text: Farms here, in what are now Tunisia, Algeria and Libya, grew much of the wheat for Rome’s bread. Lions lived wild in the hills then, but none do today.

tapTargets.pictureAlt: A dry ochre hill with thorn bushes and one olive tree, above a strip of golden wheat fields and blue sea.

framingDevice.label: SOON AFTER THIS STORY
framingDevice.line: The arena in this story was a long ground built for races. About forty years later, Rome built its greatest arena of all.

tapTargets.title: An old book
tapTargets.line: A Roman writer named Aulus Gellius wrote this story down about 1,850 years ago.

cultureNote.label: From ancient Rome
cultureNote.text: Gellius said the story came from a man who watched it happen in Rome. Nobody can check that now, so we cannot be sure how much of it is true.

tapTargets.pictureAlt: A half-open scroll with lines of small dark writing, with a reed pen and a little inkpot beside it.

paras: ^<name:androcles>Androcles</name> was a <tap:slavery>slave</tap> in a hot white town beside the sea.
He baked his master’s bread before dawn and carried his master’s water at noon. He owned nothing, not even his own two feet.
His master was a hard man with a hard voice. “Faster!” was the kindest word he ever said.
One night, when the house was asleep, Androcles lifted the bar of the gate. The hinge creaked. A dog turned over in its sleep.
Then he ran, past the last wall and the last olive tree, up into the dry hills where no road went.
By noon the rocks were too hot to touch. His water skin was empty, and his tongue felt like a strip of leather.
Far below lay the yellow wheat fields and the blue sea. Rome’s <tap:empire-moment>empire</tap> ruled every shore of that sea, and its soldiers hunted runaway slaves on all of them.
<say:androcles*>“Then I must go where soldiers will not,”</say> said Androcles, and he climbed higher.
Among the thorn bushes he found a cave. Inside, it was dim and cool, and the floor was soft sand. He lay down just to rest his eyes, and slept like a stone.
A sound woke him: a low, rough groan, close by.
The mouth of the cave had gone dark. A <name:lion>lion</name> stood in it, a lion with a black mane that hung to his knees. There was no other way out.
Androcles pressed his back to the rock and waited for the spring. It did not come.
The Lion limped in on three legs. Then he sat down and held out one great paw, the way a child shows a splinter.
The paw was swollen as round as a loaf. Deep in the pad stuck a thorn as long as a finger.
<say:androcles*>“So that is your trouble,”</say> whispered Androcles. <say:androcles>“I have had thorns of my own.”</say>
His hands shook. He crept forward and took the heavy paw into his lap. It burned against his knees.
He gripped the thorn with his finger and thumb. <say:androcles*>“Hold still, now. One, two…”</say>
He <stretch>pulled</stretch>. Out came the thorn, and the Lion <pop:1.3>roared</pop> so that dust fell from the roof. Androcles shut his eyes.
Something warm and wet rasped across his hand, rough as a scrubbing brush. The Lion was licking him. Androcles laughed out loud, tore a strip from his tunic, and bound the paw up tight.
So began the strangest household in all <tap:north-africa>North Africa</tap>.
Each morning the Lion went hunting over the hills. Each evening he came back and laid the best of his catch at the man’s feet, like a guest bringing a gift.
Androcles had no fire. He laid his share on a flat rock and let the noon sun cook it.
At night the hills grew cold. Then he slept against the Lion’s side, which was as warm as an oven and rumbled with every breath.
<say:androcles*>“Nobody shouts ‘Faster!’ here,”</say> Androcles told him. The Lion yawned. Three summers went by like that.
^But a lion never answers, and <name:androcles>Androcles</name> grew hungry for voices.
One morning he scratched the Lion behind the ears and walked down toward the wheat fields. He only wanted to hear people talk about the weather.
He heard soldiers instead. They looked at his torn tunic and bare feet. “A runaway,” said their captain, and tied his wrists.

The law for runaways was cruel. Androcles was put on a grain ship and sent across the sea to Rome. There he must stand in the <tap:arena-moment>arena</tap>, the ring of sand where all Rome came to watch, and face a wild beast with empty hands.
The noise reached him first. Rome was shouting, and it sounded like the sea in a storm.

A guard pushed him through a door into white sunlight. Sand stretched away on every side, raked as smooth as a tablecloth. Above the high wall sat more people than Androcles had seen in his whole life.
In a shaded box, under a purple cloth, sat the <name:emperor>Emperor</name>. He lifted one finger.
The shouting stopped. Across the sand a gate rattled up. Androcles looked at his hands. No stick, no stone, not so much as a thorn.
Out came a lion. He was huge and thin, for his keepers had kept him hungry, and he crossed the sand in great leaps.
Androcles stood still. A ring has no corners to hide in.
Ten steps away, the lion stopped. His nose went up. He sniffed the air, once, twice. Then he made a low, rough sound that Androcles knew.
The great beast lay down in the sand and licked the man’s dusty feet. Androcles dropped to his knees and put both arms round the black mane.
<say:androcles*>“It is you!”</say> he said. <say:androcles>“They caught you too, old friend. How is the paw?”</say>
For one breath all Rome was silent. Then the crowd was on its feet, roaring louder than any lion.
The Emperor sent for Androcles. <say:emperor*>“That is the fiercest lion in Rome,”</say> he said. <say:emperor>“Why does he spare you?”</say>
So Androcles told him about the cave, the thorn and the three summers. The story was written in big letters on a board and carried round the arena for all to read.
“Free the man! Free the lion!” shouted the people, row after row.
The Emperor looked at the lion leaning against the man’s legs. <say:emperor*>“Rome has spoken,”</say> he said. <say:emperor>“From today, nobody owns either of you.”</say>
After that, the two of them were seen all over Rome.
Androcles wore a clean tunic. The <name:lion>Lion</name> walked beside him on a leash as thin as a ribbon, which he could have snapped with one yawn.
Bakers ran out with coins for the man. Children leaned from windows and threw flowers, until the black mane was pink with petals.

Wherever they went, people nudged each other and pointed. An <tap:old-book>old book</tap> still keeps what they said: “There goes the lion who was a man’s friend, and the man who was a lion’s doctor.”
The Lion paid no attention. He had smelled the butcher’s shop.

landmarks.name: Colosseum

built.note: Begun under the emperor Vespasian and opened by his son Titus in 80 CE. The exact start year (70 to 72 CE) is to verify (CONTENT_PLAN §5).

low.line: A huge oval of pale stone in Rome, with rows and rows of arches.

medium.line: Rome’s greatest arena, opened about 1,950 years ago, had seats for about 50,000 people.
medium.note: Two emperors, Vespasian and his son Titus, built it between 70 and 80 CE. People and animals were made to fight there; today it stands as a place to remember.

advanced.line: An oval arena of stone, brick and concrete, built in Rome between 70 and 80 CE, with three rows of arches round the outside.
advanced.note: Roman writers describe the shows held in it. Earthquakes, and builders who carried off its stone, brought down much of one side, which is why it looks broken today.

art.alt: A great oval arena of pale stone with three rows of arches, one side standing higher than the other, under a warm sky.

landmarks.rights: Our own illustration; no photograph. Concept art drawn in code (see ART_PLACEHOLDERS.md). Landmark image rights review pending (PRD Q29). Sensitive history: the cards say plainly, without detail, that people and animals were made to fight there (CONTENT_PLAN CQ9).

landmarks.name: Temple of Artemis at Ephesus

built.note: The first great marble temple rose about 550 BCE and was burned down; a new one was begun about 323 BCE. Both dates are approximate.

low.line: A marble temple with more than 100 tall columns. It is gone now; one column stands.

medium.line: A great marble temple at Ephesus, in today’s Türkiye, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
medium.note: The first great temple rose about 550 BCE and burned down; a new one was begun about 323 BCE. It is lost now, and one rebuilt column marks the place.

advanced.line: A lost wonder: ancient writers describe a very wide marble temple ringed by more than 100 tall columns.
advanced.note: Nobody alive has seen it. Our picture follows the old descriptions and the stones dug up at Ephesus, so parts of it are a careful guess.

art.alt: A drawing of how the temple may have looked: a very wide marble temple with a forest of tall columns and a low triangular roof front, on a stepped base.

sourceNotes: This is our own retelling, written for Omramo, of the old Roman tale of Androcles and the lion.
It is not the wording of any earlier edition.
Documented source for the tale: Joseph Jacobs, "The Fables of Aesop" (1894), fable "Androcles",
Project Gutenberg ebook #28, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/28
Also: Joseph Jacobs, "Europa's Fairy Book" (1916), Project Gutenberg ebook #26019,
https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26019 (both US public domain; other territories not verified).
Source read: the Jacobs 1894 fable was read from the mirror (gutenberg.pglaf.org/2/28/28-0.txt).
Europa's Fairy Book (#26019) was NOT read; the source-check agent should compare it.
The Jacobs fable is one short paragraph. Most of our detail follows the oldest account instead:
Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 5, chapter 14 (about 170-180 CE), who gives it from Apion.
Written from knowledge of Gellius, not with the Latin or a translation open. A reviewer must check:
the three years in the cave; the meat dried in the sun with no fire; the slave sent to Rome from
the province of Africa; the story written on a board and carried round the arena; the thin leash;
the coins and flowers in the streets; and the closing saying, which is our paraphrase of Gellius.
Departures from Jacobs: he sets the meeting in a forest and has the lion lead the man to its cave;
we follow Gellius (the man shelters in the lion's cave in the hills of Roman North Africa).
Jacobs frees the lion to its forest; we follow Gellius (man and lion walk the streets of Rome).
Jacobs has the man sentenced to face that very lion; in ours, as in Gellius, the meeting is chance.
Our own inventions: Androcles as a baker; the master's word "Faster!"; the gate, hinge and dog;
the reason he leaves the cave (lonely for voices; Gellius says he grew tired of the wild life);
all spoken lines; bakers and children in the last scene; the butcher's shop at the very end.
The emperor is not named: the old account says only "Caesar" and writers disagree on which one.
Softened for ability age 8 to 10: slavery is said plainly in two sentences, with no beating shown
(Gellius speaks of daily floggings); the arena shows no fighting, no other victims and no blood;
the sentence is given as "face a wild beast with empty hands"; the lion's hunting is only "his catch".
Left out: the master's rank (a proconsul), the other beasts in the show, and Apion's name.
Plan change: the plan put two tap words on page 1 (slave, empire). One tap a page is the rule, so
"empire" is tapped on page 2. "North Africa" is tapped on page 5.
Facts in cards to check: Gellius wrote about 1,850 years ago; wheat for Rome from North Africa;
no wild lions in North Africa today; slavery unlawful in every country today; Colosseum 70-80 CE,
about 50,000 seats; Temple of Artemis about 550 BCE, rebuilt from about 323 BCE, 100+ columns.
The arena of the tale is the Circus Maximus in Gellius; the Colosseum opened about 40 years later.
SOURCE CHECK (18 Nov 2026, against Gutenberg #28 and #26019 on the mirror): no echo of Jacobs found.
Departures from 'Europa's Fairy Book' (not read by the writer): there the forest is near Rome, the lion
brings a young deer, the master takes Androcles to the authorities, he has a spear in the arena (ours:
empty hands), and the lion is sent back to the forest. From memory of Gellius (to verify): the people
vote the lion to Androclus as a gift; our Emperor says 'nobody owns either of you', which is ours.
Jacobs's note prints 'Appian' for Apion and says he borrowed touches from Caxton.
The Colosseum card label reads 'SOON AFTER THIS STORY' (about forty years), not 'LONG AFTER'.

palette.mood: Mediterranean and sun-bleached: pale blue-gold sky, ochre rock, terracotta, dusty olive green, and the lion's tawny gold with a near-black mane. Quiet and warm, a little dusty; one note of red or purple cloth per picture.

artBrief.light: Strong, clear daylight in every picture, one warm light from the upper left, short soft shadows. LIGHT theme: every scene keeps a PALE sky or pale sunlit rock or wall behind the words. No night scene: the night escape of page 1 is told in words only, over the pale hills scene. The cave is seen from OUTSIDE, in sunlight; only the cave mouth itself is a soft dark shape, on the trailing half.
world: Time and place: the Roman Empire about 40 CE. Part I is in the province of Africa (today's Tunisia and nearby): dry limestone and ochre hills, thorn scrub, a few grey-green olive trees, dwarf palms, and far below a plain of golden wheat running to a blue sea.
The town of page 1 (far off, small, if drawn at all): low whitewashed and ochre houses with flat or low tiled roofs beside the sea. No domes, no minarets, no pointed arches.

Androcles's dress: a short, rough, undyed wool tunic to the knee, belted with a cord, torn at the hem after the thorn scene (he tears a strip off it). Bare feet in Part I. A goatskin water bag on a strap. In the last scene a clean pale tunic and simple leather sandals.

The Lion is a Barbary lion, the North African lion: very big, tawny, with a long dark brown to black mane that runs down the chest and along the belly. Thin and rangy in the arena scenes. Never snarling at the viewer; his moods are pain, patience, sleepiness and gladness.

The thorn: one long pale acacia-type thorn, about the length of a finger, in the pad of a front paw. The paw is swollen but there is no blood. The bandage is a strip of the same undyed cloth as the tunic.
Soldiers (page 6, only if drawn, small and far): plain tunics, cloaks, oval or rectangular shields, simple round helmets, spears. No plumed parade helmets.

The arena is NOT the Colosseum, which was not yet built. Draw a long racing ground like the Circus Maximus: a long curve of pale raked sand, a plain high wall round it, stone seats low down and wooden stands above, striped or plain cloth awnings on poles, tiers of tiny spectators as dots of white, ochre and red. A barred wooden gate in the wall.

The Emperor's box: a roofed stone box in the stands with a purple cloth hung over its front rail and two plain columns. The Emperor is a small figure in a white toga with a broad purple border and a thin gold wreath. He is not any one emperor: no portrait likeness.
The board of page 9: a plain whitened wooden board on a pole with a few lines of dark capital letters (not readable), carried by one attendant along the foot of the wall.

The Roman street: three- and four-storey houses with stuccoed walls in ochre, cream and deep red, low terracotta tiled roofs, wooden shutters, shop fronts open to the street with stone counters and cloth awnings, big paving stones, a small stone fountain with a spout. Round loaves of bread scored into wedges on a baker's counter.

People of Rome: plain knee-length tunics for most, in undyed, ochre, brown and dull blue; long dresses and shawls for women; a toga on only one or two men. Skin tones mixed, as in a city that drew people from every shore of the sea. Flowers thrown are small pink and red roses and petals.
The leash is a thin cord or ribbon, slack, held lightly; no chain, no collar with spikes, no cage in any scene.

Avoid: the Colosseum or any four-storey arcaded oval; gladiators, gladiator helmets, swords, nets and tridents as decoration; chariots racing; blood, whips, chains, crosses or any cruelty imagery; other victims or other beasts; medieval dress, castles, knights; a savannah with flat-topped acacia trees, giraffes or zebras (this is North Africa, not East Africa); a short-maned East African lion; white marble everywhere (Roman streets were painted stucco and brick).

characters.androcles: A wiry man of Roman North Africa, about thirty: warm brown skin, dark curly hair cut short, a short dark beard, strong forearms dusted with flour in the first picture if he is shown at home. Short rough undyed tunic with a cord belt, bare feet; a clean pale tunic and sandals in the street scene. Signature detail: the long thorn held up between finger and thumb, and the torn hem of his tunic.
characters.lion: A very big Barbary lion, tawny gold, with a heavy near-black mane down his chest and under his belly, a broad nose and small plain amber eyes. Signature detail: one front paw held out, later wrapped in a strip of pale cloth. Thin in the arena; sleek, with petals in his mane, in the street.
characters.emperor: A small upright figure in his shaded box: clean-shaven, short dark hair, white toga with a broad purple border, a thin gold wreath. Signature gesture: one lifted finger. Calm and curious, not cruel; not a likeness of any real emperor.

scene-hills.unfolded: Far: a pale blue sky warming to gold at the horizon, a thin strip of blue sea and a band of golden wheat plain, low across both panes. Middle: folds of dry ochre hill with dots of thorn scrub. Near, on the trailing (right) half: hot ochre rocks, a thorn bush, one twisted olive tree, and Androcles hurrying uphill with his water skin, looking back over his shoulder. The leading (left) pane's upper two thirds are calm pale sky above the far plain.
scene-hills.folded: Androcles in the middle, climbing among ochre rocks and thorn bushes, head turned to look back; the far sea a thin blue line behind him and pale sky above for the words.

scene-cave.unfolded: Seen from outside in full sun. Far: pale gold sky and a far ochre ridge. Middle and near, on the trailing (right) half: a wall of warm rock with the soft dark mouth of the cave, thorn bushes beside it; in front of the mouth the big Lion sitting, one front paw held out, and Androcles kneeling to him with the paw in his lap. The leading (left) pane's upper two thirds are pale sky above a low line of pale sunlit rock.
scene-cave.folded: Close on the two of them at the cave mouth: Androcles's bent head and steady hands in the middle, the great paw in his lap, the Lion's dark mane and patient face beside him, pale sunlit rock above for the words.

scene-arena.unfolded: Far: a pale bright sky. Middle: the long curve of the arena wall running across both panes, plain and high, with tiers of tiny spectators and cloth awnings above it; on the trailing (right) half the Emperor's shaded box with its purple cloth, and a barred gate low in the wall. Near, on the trailing half: a wide floor of pale raked sand with the man and the lion small and alone on it, a few steps apart, short shadows under them. The leading (left) pane's upper two thirds are pale sky above the far, low line of the stands. This is a long racing ground, not the Colosseum.
scene-arena.folded: Androcles in the middle on the pale sand, seen from a little behind, facing the lion a few steps away; the high wall and a row of tiny spectators across the top of the band, pale sky above.

scene-street.unfolded: Far: a pale morning sky and a jumble of low tiled roofs. Middle, on the trailing (right) half: a street of ochre and red stuccoed houses with open shop fronts and awnings, a baker's counter with round loaves, a stone fountain, people leaning from upper windows throwing flowers. Near, on the trailing half: Androcles in his clean tunic walking with the Lion on a slack thin leash, petals in the dark mane and on the paving stones. The leading (left) pane's upper two thirds are pale sky above one low, plain cream wall.
scene-street.folded: Androcles and the Lion in the middle, walking toward us side by side, the thin leash slack between them, petals falling, a shop awning and a pale wall behind.

pictures.slavery: One heavy wooden house gate standing a little open with its iron bar lying on the ground beside it, and pale morning light in the gap; no people. Quiet, not grim.
pictures.north-africa: One dry ochre hill with thorn bushes and a single olive tree, centred, above a strip of golden wheat and a strip of blue sea.
pictures.old-book: One half-open papyrus scroll on two wooden rods, centred, with lines of small dark writing (not readable), a reed pen and a small round inkpot beside it. Roman books were scrolls; do not draw a bound book.

portraits.androcles: Half figure, a small relieved smile, in his rough tunic, holding the long thorn up between finger and thumb; warm pale ochre rock behind.
portraits.lion: The Lion sitting up, seen from the front, dark mane framing a calm face, one front paw raised and wrapped in a strip of pale cloth; warm gold light behind.

artBrief.cover: The thorn moment, in the middle of the picture: Androcles kneeling with the Lion's great paw in his lap, his fingers on the thorn, the Lion's dark-maned head bent to watch; the cave mouth in warm ochre rock behind them and pale gold sky above.

landmarks.colosseum: Our own drawing of the Colosseum as it stands today, by day under a warm sky: the great oval of pale travertine with three rows of arches and the plain top storey, the outer ring standing full height on one side and broken down to the inner arches on the other. No crowds, no fighting. No photograph traced.
landmarks.temple-of-artemis-ephesus: A drawing of how the temple may have looked, clearly a reconstruction: a very wide marble temple on a stepped base with a double row of tall fluted Ionic columns (scroll-shaped tops) across the front and down the sides, and a low triangular roof front, under a clear sky. No statue of the goddess; architecture only. No photograph traced.
